solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Fix a soft drink first to dilute a cocktail

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: to pin = to fix in place

explanation.surface: A barman watering down a cocktail by pouring in a soft drink first.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to read 'dilute' as a verb; it only gives up its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by name: a rum, pineapple and coconut drink is one of the best-known cocktails.

clue.text: Piano provided to introduce a singer

explanation.surface: A pianist accompanying a singer as she is introduced on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical surface keeps 'piano' looking like an instrument rather than a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Édith Piaf was the French singer of 'Non, je ne regrette rien'.

clue.text: Drama over a lost cause

explanation.surface: A play about someone who is beyond help.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is 'a' = PER, as in prices; 'over a lost cause' reads as one phrase but splits after 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: someone with no hope of success is a lost cause.

clue.text: A revolt about jam sandwiches in school

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way
a sandwich holds a filling between two slices

blocks.note: conserve = jam; it splits CONSERV…E round the rest
a riot is a revolt; 'about' turns it into TOIR

explanation.surface: Pupils rioting over the jam sandwiches at school lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Jam sandwiches look like food; here 'jam' is the bread, holding A TOIR as the filling.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowed French word for a specialist school, usually of music or drama.

clue.text: Coffee retail, extremely variable in recent times

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only R and L of 'retail' are used

explanation.surface: A complaint that coffee prices have swung wildly lately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely variable' looks like one phrase about prices; 'extremely' belongs to 'retail' and 'variable' is just Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the latter is the more recent, so the adverb means of late.

clue.text: Cow’s too thin, diameter not good

blocks.note: d = diameter; this letter comes in

explanation.surface: A worried farmer: the cow is underweight and in bad shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' is a verb, to intimidate, not the animal the surface shows.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to cow someone is to frighten them into submission.

clue.text: Bitter leaves off bay tree

indicators.note: to leave something off is to omit it

blocks.note: acerb = sour, bitter, as in acerbic
b = bay; removed from the end

explanation.surface: Bitter-tasting leaves stripped from a bay tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' and 'bay tree' paint a picture of foliage; 'leaves' is really a verb, and the tree is not the bay.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by genus: Acer is the botanical name for the maples, and gardeners call a Japanese maple an acer.

clue.text: Splits in two sticks

blocks.note: the older verb, as in 'a man shall cleave unto his wife'

explanation.surface: Someone snapping sticks in half.
explanation.walkthrough: One verb with two opposite meanings, split apart and cling together; 'sticks' reads as a noun but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two unrelated Old English verbs merged into one spelling: one means to split, the other to cling.

clue.text: Caine — not one involved with screen revival

indicators.note: one is I, the Roman numeral, so CAINE goes without its I
to be involved is to be tangled up

explanation.surface: Michael Caine's film career making a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a screen revival for the actor Michael Caine, which is exactly what the definition says.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: from Latin renasci, to be born again, the same root as renaissance.

clue.text: Layer put on when making pasty

indicators.note: in an across answer, putting one piece on another means adding it after

explanation.surface: A baker laying pastry over the filling to make a pasty.
explanation.walkthrough: A layer is a hen here, the one that lays; 'pasty' is the adjective, pale, not the pie the surface shows.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective synonym: both describe a pale, grey, unhealthy face, the colour of ash or of dough.

clue.text: Club star regularly skipped meal, but not starter

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter of 'star' is taken
the letters jumped over, S and A, are left out
a starter is what comes first, so LUNCHEON loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A club's star player who skipped the starter at a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starter' pretends to be a first course; here it is the first letter. 'Club' is a weapon, not the team.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by type: a short heavy stick carried by British police, one kind of club.

clue.text: Do or don’t top your hot dog?

blocks.note: 'that will do' = that is good enough
read literally: leave the condiment off

explanation.surface: A question at the hot-dog stand: mustard or no mustard?
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to be good enough; the second half reads it literally, with 'cut' as leave out.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for being up to standard, set against a literal reading of cutting (omitting) a hot-dog topping.

clue.text: Private events actively fending off drugs

indicators.note: something active is on the move, so the letters are set moving into a new order

explanation.surface: A private party working hard to keep drugs out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'fending off drugs' as keeping drugs away; the definition is drugs that fend off, that is, disease.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical sense: drugs taken to ward off illness rather than cure it.

clue.text: Look, a reindeer mostly eats veg

indicators.note: most but not all of a word, so PRANCER loses its last letter
what is eaten goes inside

blocks.note: Prancer, one of Santa's reindeer, without its last letter
a pea is a vegetable; it goes inside PRANCE

explanation.surface: Look, a reindeer is munching its vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look' seems to be an exclamation; it is the definition. The reindeer is a named one, Prancer.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: someone's look, as in 'I don't like the look of him', is how they appear.

clue.text: Team, Liverpool, say, bitter having let in five

indicators.note: a team that lets in goals takes them inside its net

blocks.note: Liverpool is an example of a port
bitter is a type of beer; it holds V

explanation.surface: A bitter Liverpool team after conceding five goals.
explanation.walkthrough: Liverpool looks like the team; it is only an example of a port, and 'bitter' is beer, not a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Port Vale is a football club from Stoke-on-Trent.

clue.text: Ran after being pronounced innocent

indicators.note: to pronounce a word is to say it, so it is the sound that counts, not the spelling

explanation.surface: A suspect who fled after being declared not guilty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pronounced innocent' reads as a verdict; 'pronounced' is the sound signal and 'innocent' means pure.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral synonym: sexually pure, innocent of wrongdoing.

clue.text: Economic area’s lament when turning to gas

indicators.note: to turn is to face the other way

blocks.note: to rue = to regret, lament; turned round

explanation.surface: An economic region complaining as it switches its energy to gas.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about energy policy; 'gas' is simply ozone.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the group of EU countries sharing the euro as currency form one economic area.

clue.text: Hapless chap trapped by changes in rules

indicators.note: 'hapless' split as HAP-less means CHAP minus HAP
what is trapped is held inside

explanation.surface: An unlucky man caught out by changes in the regulations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hapless' reads as unlucky; split it: HAP-less, so CHAP loses HAP.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun synonym: an edict is an official order or decree, a rule laid down by authority.

clue.text: One new around Rome after migrating?

definitions.text: One new around Rome after migrating?

indicators.note: things that migrate move somewhere else, so ROME's letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: A newcomer settling in Rome after moving there.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too. 'Around' is C, circa, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: The &lit reads straight: someone newly arrived around Rome after migrating is one who has come in.

clue.text: Plant workers’ group jolly to Morecambe?

blocks.note: a jolly is slang for a Royal Marine
Eric Morecambe, the British comedian of Morecambe and Wise

explanation.surface: A factory union's jolly outing to the seaside town of Morecambe.
explanation.walkthrough: Morecambe is a Lancashire seaside resort, which suits a works outing, but here it names the comedian. 'Plant' looks like a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by type: the yellow spice comes from the root of a plant in the ginger family.

clue.text: Raised on French, Welsh girl’s native language

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting a word writes it bottom to top

blocks.note: Siân is a Welsh girl's name

explanation.surface: A Welsh girl brought up speaking French as well as her mother tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has you thinking of Welsh as the native language; the answer is neither Welsh nor French.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the mother tongue of people from Russia.

clue.text: Amusement mounts as music hero sings out

indicators.note: out as in out of order, so the letters of HERO SINGS are rearranged

explanation.surface: A music hero belting out songs at a fairground ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music hero' looks like a single idea, a rock star; split it after 'music'. 'Sings out' seems to be one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful description: toy horses a child mounts and rocks for fun.

clue.text: Leave before rubbish is suggested

indicators.note: what comes before is written first, so the leaving word precedes the rubbish word

explanation.surface: Advice to leave before the rubbish arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters re-split across the word break, as in 'what was being got at'. 'Is' just joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: what someone is getting at is what they are hinting, so what is got at is suggested.

clue.text: Yield protected by finance department

indicators.note: what is protected is held safe inside, so the answer lies within the next two words

blocks.note: straddles the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: Profits kept safe by the finance department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yield' looks like a return on investment, which suits the finance department; here it is a verb, to give up.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to give up territory or a point is to yield it.

clue.text: Deputy, less sensible, outspoken as well

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so 'too' is heard as the number

blocks.note: numb-er = more numb, with less feeling

explanation.surface: A deputy who is both less sensible and too blunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less sensible' seems to mean foolish; read 'sensible' as able to feel, so NUMBER is 'more numb', not the counting word.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal title: the second in command ranks just under number one.

clue.text: Last stand

blocks.note: to tolerate, as in 'I can't stand it'

explanation.surface: A last stand, the final battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last stand' is a set phrase; both words are verbs here.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb with two senses: to remain or endure, and (usually negated) to tolerate.

clue.text: In New York this would be almost noble

indicators.note: the answer would sit in N and Y, so taking those outer letters away from the result leaves it

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation; these outer letters are removed

explanation.surface: An American aristocrat, or nearly one, in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay runs backwards: put the answer in NY and you get NEARLY, 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by rank: a British noble title between viscount and marquess.

clue.text: Late in the evening, move with the music crowd

explanation.surface: A crowd dancing late at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late in the evening' is a clock time, not a description.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporting sense: the number of people present at a match is its crowd.
